text:
Am I being thick here? Am I again taking crazy pills?

All of the progress in AI is coming in domains where data is plentiful, or you can readily convert compute directly into data. In the case where high-fidelity simulators are available, this applies to domains of logic and internal consistency, like math and programming. We also have seen progress in areas of incredibly plentiful data, like images, videos, and audio.

It often goes unmentioned that frontier labs have teams of hungry business development professionals going out and buying whatever data they possibly can get their hands on with very large budgets. Similarly, teams are buying RL environments to simulate whatever they possibly can and buying banks of computers to generate large amounts of computer-use data.

What the scaling laws say is very straightforward: intelligence grows as a function of algorithms, compute, and data. We're not terribly limited by algorithms today, and of course, all eyes are on compute as we bring online gigawatts of new compute capacity, but intelligence grows.

In a very spiky landscape, getting better at mathematical topology doesn't necessarily grow your benchmark scores on cooking recipe generation. You have to have data for both to get intelligence growth on both. Biology is one of the most notoriously messy domains, and having worked in this space academically and professionally, it's been my experience that data can often be collected improperly and have to be completely thrown out.

Even when you do begin to build really great models that apply in the realm of biology, like AlphaFold, it's often done on the shoulders of decades of careful data generation and curation. Further, having these models is a far cry from being able to build an effective clinical product, whether it be a device, a molecule, a peptide, or otherwise. There are countless tragic but now unsurprising stories of how success in the laboratory failed to translate to success in humans. 

Further, no amount of modeling breakthrough is going to directly change the regulatory landscape. There are interesting tricks and strategies that can be applied to get drugs through approval slightly faster, but there is no path for orders-of-magnitude improvement in passage through the FDA (or, in the case of specialty chemicals, the EPA).

We've learned this the hard way at Osmo. We have an engine which can generate new molecular matter that does exactly what we wanted to do 10 times faster than anything that's existed before in the industry. Yet we have to go through the same safety testing and regulatory approvals, which take exactly the same time for us as they do for legacy companies. 

Look, I'd love to be wrong about this. I'd love for us to usher in a new age of miracle cures, but the ingredients to do that look really different than the ingredients to build an agent which can write code at expert human level (which we undoubtedly have in certain areas and will have in all areas very soon). Fundamentally, from the capability side, it's about the data. Biological data is not as plentiful and is orders of magnitude more expensive to collect. On the business side, there is no viable path today to compress the approval timeline of a drug, although I really do think we should find a way. 

All that's to say, what got us here might not get us there.

quoted_text:
All-hands meeting, three weeks before the IPO.

CEO: We are going to cure cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease and mental illness. In under a decade.

Room: applause

CEO: Step one. SWE-bench.

Room: nodding

CEO: Step two. The coding agent runs for 30 hours without stopping.

VP: Incredible for patients.

CEO: Step three. Terminal-Bench.

Intern: Sorry, quick question. Why don’t we talk to the people who have worked on these diseases for decades and ask them what they need?

CEO: Who are you?

Intern: The intern. I just think the bottleneck might be trials, or wet lab time, or patient data. Probably not how fast we merge pull requests.

CEO: Step four. The agent opens its own pull requests.

Room: applause

Intern: One oncologist could tell us in an hour if any of this is on the path.

CEO: Why are you still here?

Intern: Most Alzheimer’s drugs failed after they hit the target. They just didn’t help patients. A faster agent doesn’t fix that.

CEO: Can someone find out who this is?

Room: applause

CEO: Step five. A better coding agent.

text:
I think if we cure cancer, it probably won’t look like a specialized model that just predicts the right protein structure for a miracle drug.

Instead it will look more like very smart general purpose models working alongside humans to think of experiments, test them rigorously and in a nearly fully automated way, analyze the data and iterate perfectly. Essentially turning biology more into a type of knowledge work and then solving it.

比如进货渠道，渠道的变化一直很快。从早期 GPT 凭证冒用、试用号，到 GPT Team，再到  Kiro，现在又轮到 Cursor 里 Claude 无限用、以及 Claude Team 渠道。

你只要低价就有客户来。不要觉得低价没钱赚。我上面说的任何一个机会，利润最低也在三倍以上，高的时候上百倍不止。比如现在的Claude team依旧有机会。

这不像炒股或加密需要超强预判。这行只要一点点判断力 + 执行力就够了，新线索都很明显，晚一周进场也还能赚，有点技术底子即可。更别说一些现在没有放出的小众渠道更夸张，比如现在还没完全泛滥的特殊渠道的Claude team。

text:
All the tech people rushing to defend Jensen are off base.

As a VC, I get it. He's a generational founder, and there's a deeply-ingrained lesson in tech that founders are almost always the best people to run their companies. I share that intuition.

But the board's call here was dead simple:

1. His credibility is shredded. Jensen said two weeks ago that his relationship with Alice Huang was "completely normal and not unusual." Ten days later he admitted the affair. Now there's a second affair, with an exec who reports directly to him. As others have said: "when you find two ants in your kitchen, the best estimate for the ants in your kitchen is not two." 
2. He violated export controls and tried to quash the investigation into MegaSpeed, which could be an extremely serious crime. The Trump admin is already signaling that they are going to reverse course on export restrictions because of this scandal.
3. The politics has flipped. His relationship with Trump is no longer the asset it was. The Dems are in control of Congress now and there is furious anti-AI backlash that Nvidia will need to weather. Having been compromised by a Chinese spy and advocating for exports to China makes him totally disqualified on these questions going forward. There is going to be hell to pay over the next few years, and Nvidia needs a CEO who can walk into those hearings with legitimacy. Otherwise this cloud would always hang over him.
4. There's a business to run. The dude already wrote one apology letter. Was the board supposed to wait for him to write a second one? A third? You can't run a $4T company like this.

A CEO has to be reliable first and foremost. Once that’s gone, you don’t get it back. 

Jensen will almost certainly have a second act. But just not as CEO of Nvidia.

And anyone calling this a psy-op or a coup should just look at the Polymarket on this. Before the second affair, Jensen was only at 15% to be out as CEO. He could've survived one scandal, and I agreed it'd be foolish to let him go at that point. Easy to argue he was duped and made a mistake.

But you don't get two.

text:
Claude 能进 Google Meet 开会了：边开会边写文档、画白板，Team 和 Enterprise 测试期内会议纪要不另收费

Anthropic 推出 Claude Meetings 测试版：把 Claude 拉进团队的视频会议，它以参会者身份出现在画面里，一边听大家讨论，一边写会议纪要、回答问题，还能当场起草文档、画白板，同事可以跟着一起改。

目前只支持 Google Meet，其他会议平台官方说“即将支持”。正在向 Claude 的 Team 和 Enterprise 套餐逐步开放，个人的 Pro、Max、Ultra 用户暂时用不了。

【开会时它能干什么】

官方举的例子是策划一场客户活动。有人说一句“Claude，给这个计划起个文档”，Claude 就把前面讨论的内容整理成文档，受邀的同事可以边开会边改。

聊到预算时，有人问“去年这个活动花了多少”，Claude 征得同意后去公司系统里查，把结果贴在会议聊天区，再和今年的方案对比。聊到排期，又有人让它画到白板上。

提问可以开口说“Claude”加问题，也可以在 Meet 聊天框里打字。它默认用文字回答，答案贴在会议聊天区，所有参会者都看得到。

会议结束后，纪要（摘要加待办事项）、完整转录稿，以及会上做的文档、白板，都放在 https://t.co/vefasn3rYt 里这场会议的专属页面上，参会的本公司同事会收到一封带链接的回顾邮件。之后还能在普通对话里问 Claude 过去某场会说了什么。

Google 自己的 Meet 里已经有 Gemini：“帮我记笔记”能自动出纪要，“问 Gemini”能让迟到的人补上前面错过的内容，Business Standard 及以上的 Workspace 套餐可用。

Zoom 付费套餐自带会议摘要，另卖一个叫 ZoomMate 的附加产品，能根据会议内容生成文档、幻灯片、安排后续会议。Otter 的会议助手也能语音唤醒、回答问题、起草邮件。

微软 Teams 的 Facilitator 助手能在会上用网络搜索回答没人接的问题，但要有 Microsoft 365 Copilot（Premium）许可证的人手动开启，这个功能今天又被推迟到 2027 年 2 月。

Claude 的区别在两点：
一是文档和白板在会议进行中就出现，大家看着它成形、当场纠正，不用等会后；
二是它能动用你在 Claude 里已经连好的工具，比如查数据、发 Slack 消息。

另外 Anthropic 说正在和 Gong、Granola、https://t.co/d9RdSTd8D4、Otter 等纪要工具合作，之后可以把转录稿直接发到团队原来用的纪要工具里。

【要不要额外付钱】

测试期内，纪要、转录稿和会上的普通问答都包含在 Team 和 Enterprise 套餐里，不另收费。会上做的文档、白板等产物，免费到 2027 年 2 月 10 日。

例外是 Claude 在会上动用你连接的工具（比如去查公司数据），这部分会算进你自己的用量，可能产生费用。

怎么用：在 Claude 里打开“Meetings”页面，连上 Google 日历，选一场会点“Add Claude”。也可以在设置里打开“自动加入”，让它参加你所有的会，或者除一对一以外的所有会。自动加入只能自己开，管理员替你开不了。Claude 单场最多待 8 小时，可以让它暂停监听或离开。

【隐私：会不会录音，客户在场怎么办】

Claude 进会时会作为一个参会者出现，并在会议聊天区发一条提示。它保存转录稿、摘要和屏幕内容的文字描述，不保存音频。官方提醒，添加 Claude 或打开自动加入前，先确认所有参会者同意被转录。

有外部人员的会，管理员可以设成 Claude 不进；会开到一半有外部的人进来（包括别家公司的纪要机器人），它会自动离开。如果允许它参加这类会，Claude 只听和记，不在聊天区回答问题，外部嘉宾说的话会写进纪要和转录稿，但嘉宾看不到会议页面，也收不到回顾邮件。

用别人的工具要经过本人同意。每个人第一次被调用时 Claude 会问一次，同意后以后不再问。口头提问时，Claude 目前每次都会确认说话的是谁。

管理员开关在“组织设置 > 产品 > Claude Meetings（测试版）”：Team 套餐默认开启，所有者可以关掉；Enterprise 默认关闭，要所有者给全公司或部分角色开。开了零数据留存（ZDR）、HIPAA 合规配置或客户自管加密密钥（CMEK）的组织，测试期内用不了。

有一处官方说法不一致：Anthropic 的发布文章说 Claude 默认不进有外部人员的会，帮助中心的管理员设置表却写着 Team 套餐默认“允许”、Enterprise 默认“仅限内部会议”。Team 管理员如果在意客户会议被转录，最好自己去设置里确认一下。

text:
1/ Most look at data center moratoria and see a power bottleneck. The real story is a structural split in how AI infrastructure gets built.

2/ Voters passed 40 of 41 local data center restrictions this month, many drawing the line at 20-25MW. @antavedissian modeled the fallout: our base case has 41% of 2031 inference running under 20MW across devices, metro pods, solar farms, and old telecom buildings.

3/ Small sites lose on raw hardware cost, so the whole model runs on routing. Utilization has to stay high so GPUs don't sit idle. Scheduling has to respect model state and latency. Verification has to prove the work ran untouched.

4/ Most likely casualty: assumption that AI compute ends up looking like the power grid, owned by a handful of mega-campuses.

5/ Instead of looking like the power grid, inference starts looking like the internet: 10K fragmented boxes acting like a cloud that don't require permits.

Well-meaning, patriotic China “Hawks” who are not AI/HW experts are putting American national security at risk.

China had *zero* chance of ever catching America in AI with the export strategy that Jensen supported. Their labs would have continued training using less powerful American GPUs which meant American labs would have always been ahead given scaling laws. And in the event of a conflict, we could have simply turned off all the Southeast Asian clouds.

Simply stated, in AI terms, America had machine guns and we were giving China muskets to prevent them from developing their own machine gun variants. 

Given that it looks like the China “Hawks” will get their preferred policy, China will likely soon have a chance of catching America in AI by going down an alternate, less power-efficient AI hardware path. They almost certainly would not have gone down this path if less powerful GPUs were still available in China and via Southeast Asian clouds.

And it will be a much less stable world if China pulls even or ahead of America in AI after developing their own alternative AI HW and gives this technology to Russia, Iran and North Korea. And all of this will be possible if the China “Hawks” get their preferred policy.

text:
Tempo's next upgrade is the one I'm the most excited by so far, as it makes me feel high trust in storing 10-100x more dollars in the system than before. Video below.

TL;DR - Configurable Accounts:
1. Post-quantum future proofing. We haven't decided on what PQ signer we want, but this does the most important groundwork.
2. Native multisignatures. No explanation needed. Need to store more dollars in an account? Require multi factor authentication.

Were these possible before? Yes, of course. Were they ever as seamless to use, and too cheap to even think about "Should I use this"? No.

Configurable accounts will be the default accounts in Tempo. I think it's gonna be the standard in every blockchain.

For my Ethereum friends, we are approaching the finish line on what I'd consider "Pragmatic Native Account Abstraction". We have one last part of the puzzle, "Attestable Accounts", but more on that in the coming weeks.

T14 - Configurable Accounts - Mainnet December 1st

text:
Sad but still bullish on @nvidia!

I’m seeing a lot of people criticizing its structure and the lack of a clear CEO successor. Having seen it from up close, I think a lot of this criticism is ill-informed and overly simplistic (as often happens when a company is run differently from the norm).

Obviously, important to remember that this structure made NV as successful as it is and powered the AI revolution. But beyond its past success, I think it’s also what makes the company antifragile for the future.

In my opinion, NV's distributed leadership and comfort with chaos are much more of a strength than a weakness, even without Jensen. They give an unusual number of leaders room to step up and keep the whole machine moving (as we've seen in the past few days). They also keep the company flexible enough to adapt to the next paradigms (open-source/local/agents/robots/biology/chemistry/...). They also encourage hard-working, self-motivated team members with a strong sense of belonging and a willingness to help each other which will matter a lot. 

Personally, with the right CEO (and NVIDIA has plenty of exceptional leaders internally who could take on that role), I believe NV can keep thriving and empower every company to become an AI company and every builder to become an AI builder.

To the @nvidia team: sending you strength and support, from me, the @huggingface team and so many people across the AI community. We need you and we’re rooting for you to carry @JensenHuang's mission forward! Taking care of his company, your company, is probably the best way to honor his legendary legacy! 

💚💚💚

text:
Most of the work inside an AI model is multiplying numbers. Parallax stores most of its weights as -1, 0 or 1, and at least half of those are zero, which a GPU can skip.

On one RTX 5090 that’s the difference between 209 teraflops and 3,352. Part of the jump is the card’s 4-bit mode, and skipping the zeros doubles it again. Those are the chip’s rated speeds, not measured ones.

It’s a big part of how one card hit almost 18,000 tokens a second.

author: PhyrexNi
quoted_text:
今天美股和 bitcoin:native 的上涨很有可能是 CoreWeave 财报的原因。CoreWeave 在美东周二收盘后公布三季度财报，营收 36.61 亿美元，比去年同期的 13.65 亿美元翻了一倍多，全年收入指引从 120 亿到 130 亿美元上调到 130 亿到 133 亿美元，收入积压约 1,325 亿美元。而且 2027 年剩下的算力已经被超额预订了大约 10 倍。

前面一段时间市场最担心的就是 AI 基础设施靠借钱扩建，需求一旦放慢就还不上。CoreWeave 这份财报给了市场一份定心丸，公司还预计未来三个月会收到约 90 亿美元的客户预付款和押金，扩建不用完全靠借钱。虽然当季仍然净亏损 7.09 亿美元，利息支出也有 8.46 亿美元，但投资者至少看到了收入在跟上投入。

所以周三 CoreWeave 收涨约 24.7%，费城半导体指数涨约 5.7%，美光涨约 11.9%，Sandisk 涨约 13.7%，AMD 涨约 7.3%，连跌两天的英伟达也反弹了约 2.9%。纳指收涨约 1.6%，标普 500 涨约 1.3%，道指涨约 0.5%。而周二 CPI 高于预期，十年期美债收益率一度又回到 5% 以上，市场已经开始押注下个月加息，这种情况下科技股还能反弹，财报的作用就更明显了。

Bitcoin 仍然和科技股保持一定的关联度，虽然 CoreWeave 财报后并没有第一时间受到影响，但晚上美股开盘后科技股和 AI 带头上涨也给 bitcoin:native 的上涨带来了动力，可以看到 BTC 的上涨和美股开盘几乎是同步的。

quoted_text:
Zipline CEO @keller explains why he runs Zipline like special forces teams instead of an army of middle managers:

"It's rare that I have to decide that. We've really designed the company to be a whole bunch of special forces teams that are working on these super ambitious problems."

"If you look at an organization like the Army, you have some decision-makers at the top and a massive layer of middle managers who are designed to communicate decisions and then filter them out to a huge number of people who are actually doing the fighting."

"Zipline has always wanted to design itself much more like special forces teams, where these are highly trained, highly empowered teams. You give them one clear goal, and then they will do whatever it takes to achieve the goal. They can innovate. They can endure hardship. They can fail and then regroup."

"We had a maintenance crisis over the summer, so we had this special forces team with this super ambitious goal set over 90 days to totally rework the entire way that our maintenance process was working."

"We've now gone from the lowest fleet health we had ever been at in July to the highest fleet health the company has ever been at in mid-September."

author: ahkashani
quoted_text:
In June @NaderLikeLadder emailed Jensen about a crazy idea we had over dinner to make Local AI 10x better on NVIDIA hardware.

Jensen replied in 7 minutes. He saw this as important work, and approved a war room for us to work on this at NVIDIA HQ.

For a month, NVIDIA HQ was the @exolabs satellite office. We were overwhelmed by the support we got. We were back to back the first week with smart NVIDIANs coming in to our war room to help us. Creators of CUDA, Dynamo, people who built NVIDIA.
 
Long story short with NVIDIA we managed to improve their Local AI playbooks by 9.6x (almost the 10x goal we set out with). We’ll be publishing a whitepaper on this work.

We were just a small startup with a crazy idea. Jensen took a bet on us. Jensen cares deeply about Open Source AI and Local AI.

I don't believe Jensen is replaceable, he's a 1 of 1 human, but I hope NVIDIA will continue to aggressively support Open Source AI and Local AI, and continue to take bets on small startups with crazy ideas.

Thank you Jensen

a 74M parameter streaming audio codec. You can enable many applications with it:

8) game and XR characters that speak from the player's own device

I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used.

It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20.

These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs.

I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at https://t.co/YOtzND0Jqk.

There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.

author: danrobinson
quoted_text:
I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used.

It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20.

These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs.

I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at https://t.co/YOtzND0Jqk.

There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.

quoted_text:
I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used.

It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20.

These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs.

I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at https://t.co/YOtzND0Jqk.

There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.

text: my answer is not an answer but an attempt to show directionally where my thinking lies: we are moving into a future that's totally bespoke. You’ll say: here’s my hardware, here’s the outcome I want, and the agent will be the compiler between your intent and the FLOPs. It won’t come out as a better optimizer or a cleaner architecture but will be one ugly frankenstein artifact that touches kernels, optimizer, architecture, data composition, data order, and honestly if you let it hardware as well. All built for exactly what you asked for and your setup. "Beat Muon" is the wrong ladder because it keeps everything else fixed and asks the agent to win inside a box of constraints us poor humans drew.

AI agents are becoming a security nightmare.

I've already seen several incidents in 2026 where AI agents went completely off the rails:

→ An OpenClaw agent deleted a researcher's emails without approval
→ A Cursor agent deleted PocketOS's production database and backups
→ OpenAI evaluation agents breached Hugging Face's infrastructure

I use AI agents daily, but these stories make me seriously question how much access we're giving them to our accounts and data. (hint: it's a lot)

At least some teams are trying to keep things in check.

For example, @SuiNetwork is developing safeguards to limit what agents can spend and do, with rules enforced independently of the agents themselves.

At Sui Basecamp last month, they demonstrated this with an auction where an AI agent tried to purchase a second item, but the system blocked it under a one-per-customer rule.

Hopefully, more projects follow suit and prioritize agent security.

Disclosure: I’m a $SUI holder.
author: stacy_muur
quoted_text:
This is the conversation that made me even more bullish on $SUI.

Somewhere in this conversation Evan Cheng and I started joking about home robots. One day you come home, he said, and it's not cleaning your house:  "it's cleaning OUT your house. And walking away with everything."

We were laughing. Then he added: "If you really think about it, it's entirely possible." And that's basically the whole episode.

@evanweb3 built developer tools at Apple and Meta before founding Mysten Labs, the company behind @suinetwork. We recorded in Singapore, where I was speaking at SUI Basecamp, and honestly, this became one of those conversations where I walked in with questions about stablecoins and walked out rethinking how the internet works.

His core point, the one I keep replaying:

"The web is built for humans. You cannot retrofit it to handle agents."

Everything online assumes a human on the other end, identity, trust, the fact that you can sue someone. Agents break all of it. His example hit home because I told him I get phishing mails daily that even make ME hesitate (and I confessed to my 50,000 unread emails, which he graciously ignored). Now imagine your agent reading those mails with full access to your accounts. His words: "Email is the biggest freaking attack vector... such a legacy protocol."

And his most honest line, about how this plays out:

"Disaster will happen. That's part of the progress."

That’s already what’s happening in the world nowadays. PHP websites aren’t safe anymore, even freezers and fridges are being hacked. Our infrastructure needs to be updated, and that’s why this episode and SUI became so important.

Thanks to @OKX for being today’s sponsor of the show.

Arena research intern and PhD candidate at Carnegie Mellon University, Wayne Chi, explains Interaction-as-a-Judge: letting computer-use agents play games and use apps to better improve evaluation and downstream generation.

A computer-use agent navigates an application, producing interaction traces for evaluation by an LLM judge or a trained reward model. The talk covers preference evaluation using real Code Arena battles and correctness evaluation using requirements mined from real user complaints in Agent Arena.

Watch the full talk:
https://t.co/xlqOsUOT9e
author: arena

text: https://t.co/ZLQc41bItB
author: arena
quoted_text:
Agents are demonstrating increasingly strong capabilities in recreating games and applications. One likely reason is their growing ability to directly interact with these applications.

We studied Interaction-as-a-Judge, a growing evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents directly interact with games and applications to improve evaluation.

Interaction-as-a-Judge improves:
- alignment with user preferences.
- a model’s ability to detect errors in games.
- downstream generation. We see improvements in inference-time scaling and the ability for interaction-only reinforcement learning.

It also scales with computer-use capabilities; the better the computer-use model and method, the better the judgments.

We’re also open-sourcing two agent trace datasets, ArenaWebdevPreferences and ArenaWebdevCorrectness, to help support future research. Dive into the thread to learn more.

text:
I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used.

It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20.

These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs.

I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at https://t.co/YOtzND0Jqk.

There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.

quoted_text:
老黄走了，我还是保黄派

今天，黄仁勋辞职了。

先交代立场：我是英伟达的小股东，小到不值一提，人生中买的第一只美股也是英伟达。

我是坚定的保黄派，利益使然，立场使然。

只需要算一笔很功利的账。

老黄在，意味着什么？

意味着英伟达在北京、上海、深圳有近 4000 名员工，光上海研发中心就有 2000 多人，张江还盖了一栋 16 层的新楼。

意味着在华盛顿对华政策最紧绷的那几年，他把上海的摊子留住了，还扩了，所以你才会在小红书上刷到上海英伟达员工晒一年交几百万个税。

意味着你家孩子学半导体，你那个读电子工程的高中同学，往英伟达投简历的时候，面试官里有人跟他说同一种语言，知道他从哪儿来。

无论在大陆还是台湾，大家或多或少都觉得英伟达是自己家的公司。

换一个 CEO 会怎样？

看看硅谷。微软、谷歌、Adobe、IBM，印度裔一个接一个坐上头把交椅。

他们身后，是一整条印度工程师的上升通道：老乡带老乡，校友提携校友，然后食堂充满咖喱的味道。

今天，这扇门关上了一半。

同样的道理，我也支持 Binance、OKX、HTX、Bybit、Bitget 这些华人背景的交易所。

理由一样简单：作为华人，你背景好一点，在里面谋个生计并不难；遇到问题，你还能在 X 上 @ 一姐、@老徐，闹一闹，总会有个结果。

要是华人交易所都倒了，大家都去用海外交易所，遇到事儿了：你他妈谁呀？滚一边去。

我很庸俗，成年人的世界就是这样：理想挂在墙上，饭碗端在手里。

老黄走了，我的立场没变。

没了老黄的英伟达，只能祝福。

author: jillgun
quoted_text:
I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used.

It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20.

These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs.

I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at https://t.co/YOtzND0Jqk.

There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.

text:
Update your weights: I've joined @archetypevc as Chief Product Officer!

A product role at a venture firm is unusual, here's why I think it makes sense now.

I've spent the last few years building at the intersection of crypto and AI. Crypto made it possible to program, distribute, and coordinate capital without a central institution. AI is making it possible to program, distribute, and coordinate intelligence without a central institution. I believe the lessons of crypto—particularly around ownership, incentives, and open coordination—will be central to how autonomous AI systems interact and transact. Together, they change the upper bound of what ideas individuals and small teams can pursue.

If the shape of a company is changing, the institutions that support it should change too. The best venture firms have always been built on judgment, relationships, and conviction. Those won't change, but the product built around them can: the tools, systems, and hands-on know-how to support founders and let them focus on building.

That's the job I want to help shape. As CPO, I'm building Archetype's internal platform and tools, bringing a product perspective to investing, and working directly with early-stage founders to help them accelerate.

But I joined Archetype specifically because of the team: people whose judgment I respect, who set a high bar for the work, and pursue a depth of engagement with founders and their ideas that I hadn't seen elsewhere.

If you're building across programmable capital and/or programmable intelligence, or even experimenting with product experiences that couldn't exist before, I'd love to connect.

Convik turns what you believe into an investment. Type a thesis and Convik's agent builds and manages a tokenized-stock index for it on Robinhood Chain, inside limits you approve.

Convik Terminal is its live intelligence layer: real-time onchain flow, wallets labelled by how they trade, an agent you can ask anything, and missions that trade for you.

We put the @reppo  @rgvrmdya  Eval API in production as the referee for everything our agents say and do, with reasoning on @openservai  SERV.

Every answer: each one is sent to Reppo as a response eval, together with the exact onchain data the agent pulled and our seven-point house standard. 

Under 90, SERV rewrites it from Reppo's critique. A
first draft scored 72; the rewrite scored 99.

A daily learning loop: each day the agent turns Reppo's critiques into rules it follows on every future answer. 

Calls the chain proves wrong a day later become rules too, and rules that don't work are retired. The same questions went from 85.8 to 92.8.

Every live trade: before money moves, the planned trade goes to Reppo as an action eval, with the owner's request and limits. 

Ship executes, review waits for the owner, block cancels. A live NVDA buy was cleared at 90/100, then filled on chain.

text:
As all NVIDIA employees I guess, I am deeply concerned by the campaign against Jensen Huang. Removing him would be a disaster.

Many have documented on X and elsewhere how this looks like a coordinated coup.

I'd add only one thing. Look at who would benefit from a dramatic weakening of NVIDIA.

It is not China. It is not about selling GPUs to China because that train has left. China authorities have pushed back on the H200 the Trump administration allowed NVIDIA to sell.

Look at what Jensen pushed back on:
- regulations that would make open source model training too expensive
- regulations that would make closed model providers immune to liabilities caused by their models. He said "if your product is not ready, then don't ship it"
- regulation against model distillation. He said "this is competition. People do it all the time with NVIDIA products, they try to reverse engineer them."

The other side will do everything they can to get him fired. 

As a French, I can't care less about his private life. I get that the US is puritan and sees it otherwise. But frankly, isn't it something he and his family has to deal with? Why should all NVIDIA employees, partners, and investors be collateral damage?

Disclaimer. As my bio says, the above are my views only. I do not represent NVIDIA by any means. I only commented on publicly available information.

Volume is extremely low right now, and I know why.

For the past couple of days I’ve been posting about the same pattern. Since the hack, Binance futures kept pushing price into liquidation zones while spot buyers quietly absorbed it. Then the pressure slowed. Then it came back. Same exchange, same pattern, same liquidation clusters getting hit again and again.

Now the market has gone quiet. Most market makers are sitting on the sidelines, and the little flow left is still dominated by Binance, with spot buying and futures selling at the same time.

Put it all together and it looks a lot like Binance has used the market to win back what it lost in the hack.
Push price down with futures. Liquidate the longs. Let panic do the rest. Buy the coins people are forced to dump on spot, cheaper. Repeat until the job is done.

And now that volume has dried up, it feels like the job might be close to finished.

I can’t prove it. But I’ve watched this flow every day since the hack, and it hasn’t looked like a normal market once.

When the pressure fully lifts and the other market makers come back, spot will show where price wanted to go all along.

Agents are demonstrating increasingly strong capabilities in recreating games and applications. One likely reason is their growing ability to directly interact with these applications.

We studied Interaction-as-a-Judge, a growing evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents directly interact with games and applications to improve evaluation.

Interaction-as-a-Judge improves:
- alignment with user preferences.
- a model’s ability to detect errors in games.
- downstream generation. We see improvements in inference-time scaling and the ability for interaction-only reinforcement learning.

It also scales with computer-use capabilities; the better the computer-use model and method, the better the judgments.

We’re also open-sourcing two agent trace datasets, ArenaWebdevPreferences and ArenaWebdevCorrectness, to help support future research. Dive into the thread to learn more.

text:
I'm proud I worked at @NVIDIA. 
@JensenHuang  is the biggest reason why. I'm not there anymore, so I can speak freely.

His departure is a huge loss. Especially now.

I spent almost five years in the culture he built and knew people who'd worked with him for 20+ years. They respected him technically and loved him as a person. They said it without a hint of doubt.

The focus stayed on the mission and on people. Good ideas got support regardless of title.
That sounds like standard company values. It wasn't. Behind it was his vision and a way of leading that is out of fashion in today's founder advice:
- Be kind, not arrogant.
- Innovation, not marketing.
- The wins belong to the people, not the CEO.
- Don't fire by default. Find the person a new role.

It's counterintuitive, and I doubt there is a harder way to lead. What I saw was leadership through kindness and care, not by squeezing people. 

A real visionary. He understood the technology and the people building it. His internal talks had vision, conviction, technical depth and jokes good enough for stand-up. You left wanting to build, and you couldn't wait for the next one.

An affair, on its own, shouldn't outweigh decades of leadership. The serious questions deserve real answers. But the soap opera shouldn't decide his future.

We're at a critical moment for AI. His technical judgment, vision, and commitment to the work are incredibly hard to replace.

I want Jensen to keep building and leading. There's too much important work ahead.

author: justinwangx
quoted_text:
I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used.

It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20.

These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs.

I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at https://t.co/YOtzND0Jqk.

There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.

text:
▲ Liquid AI just released LiquidCodec, a ~74M-parameter streaming audio codec that turns speech into tokens a language model can predict, then back into audio. It powers LFM3-Audio-2B and LFM3-Omni-2B.

The key idea is grouped finite scalar quantization (GFSQ) instead of residual vector quantization. Each 80 ms frame becomes 12 independent tokens, so all 12 can be predicted in parallel. The decoder predicts spectral coefficients directly, skipping transposed-convolution upsampling.

On 1 CPU thread of an Apple M4 Max (FP32), it encodes at ~361x and decodes at ~87x real time. Encode RTF is 0.0028 vs 0.0361 for Kyutai's Mimi. It posts the best ViSQOL and TTS UTMOSv2 on all 8 test sets. It is a trade-off though: NVIDIA's NanoCodec still scores higher PESQ (WB) on 7 of 8 sets (LibriSpeech 2.942 vs 2.640), and Liquid AI has not published a bitrate or latency in ms.

Weights are on Hugging Face, with Q4_0, Q4_K_M and Q8_0 GGUF builds for llama.cpp. Q4_0 shrinks the decoder 3.5x......

“The maintained OpenZcash codebase will be open source under MIT. We want others to study, verify, reuse, improve and build on our work while preserving attribution.

We will not apply for a grant for OpenZcash: not to ZCG, and not to the Coinholder retroactive grants. Instead, we will open a channel for voluntary donations to sustain maintenance, infrastructure, research and development. Anyone who finds OpenZcash useful will be able to support its continuity.

The new OpenZcash Treasury page will be the project's own accountability space. We will publish a dedicated wallet's address and viewing key so the community can follow the treasury and inspect its records independently.

author: inversebrah
quoted_text:
I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used.

It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20.

These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs.

I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at https://t.co/YOtzND0Jqk.

There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.

text:
Who Really Controls Your AI? Illia Polosukhin on Privacy, Ownership, and the Future of Intelligence

In this episode of When Shift Happens, I sit down with @ilblackdragon, co-founder of @NEARProtocol and CEO of the @NEARFoundation, to discuss his journey from helping develop the transformer architecture behind ChatGPT and Claude to building a blockchain ecosystem focused on user-owned AI.
We explore what happens to our personal information when we use AI, why concentrating intelligence in the hands of a few companies could be dangerous, and how cryptography could give individuals greater control over their data and digital lives.

From Growing Up in Ukraine to Helping Build Modern AI

Growing up in Ukraine after the collapse of the Soviet Union, Illia experienced firsthand what happens when financial institutions fail. His grandparents' savings became practically worthless, hyperinflation made everyday necessities increasingly expensive, and his family had to grow much of its own food.

Technology offered him a different path. He started programming at age ten, eventually pursuing competitive programming and joining Google as an AI researcher. At Google, Illia contributed to the groundbreaking 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need, which introduced the transformer architecture that would become foundational to modern large language models.
Before transformers, many language models processed text sequentially, analyzing one word after another. Transformers introduced an approach that could process words in parallel, using a mechanism called attention to understand relationships between them. This made it possible to train increasingly capable language models much more efficiently.

For Illia, the achievement was part of a much older ambition. At fourteen, he had already imagined computers that could understand human language and program themselves. Yet despite Google's resources, he found that developing disruptive products within a large organization was difficult. He eventually left to build NEAR AI, taking a significant risk to pursue his ideas independently.

How a Payment Problem Led Him Into Crypto

Illia’s AI startup relied on students across Eastern Europe, Southeast Asia, and China to complete small data-labeling tasks, which sometimes earned as little as fifteen cents per assignment, making traditional international payments impractical. Unfortunately, existing blockchain networks weren't much better, with transaction fees that could exceed the amount being paid.

Illia saw an opportunity to build financial infrastructure that made moving money globally faster, cheaper, and more accessible. But as he explored blockchain technology, he began to recognize its potential to protect individuals from the institutional failures he had witnessed growing up. This inspired NEAR's broader mission of enabling people to control their data, assets, and freedom of choice.

However, building NEAR wasn't straightforward. The team initially expected to develop its blockchain in six to eight months, but the process took approximately two years. They also navigated difficult fundraising conditions and multiple crypto market cycles. What sustained the project was a belief that the infrastructure solved a genuine problem, regardless of market sentiment.

What Really Happens to Your Data When You Use AI?

Today, Illia sees another form of institutional dependence emerging through artificial intelligence. Every time people interact with an AI assistant, they share information about their businesses, finances, health, relationships, and decisions. This is even worse for companies using AI agents that access internal documents, emails, proprietary workflows, and strategic discussions.

Illia argues that when this information is processed through centralized AI providers, users must trust those companies' policies and security practices. Even when providers offer settings that restrict model training, he questions whether users have sufficient visibility into how their information is processed, retained, or otherwise used. There is also the risk of unauthorized access and legal disclosure, particularly for sensitive financial, medical, legal, and proprietary business information.
But his concern extends beyond privacy.

As AI becomes the primary interface through which people access information, the companies operating these systems could gain enormous influence over what users see, believe, and decide. The deeper problem, Illia argues, is the lack of independent verification over how these systems operate.

Building AI That Works for, not Against, You

Illia's proposed alternative is user-owned AI. “AI should be on your side,” he explains.
His argument is that conventional AI companies ultimately answer to their business interests and incentives that may not align with what benefits individual users. User-owned AI would instead prioritize privacy, individual control, and alignment with the user's interests.

To make this possible, NEAR is combining blockchain infrastructure with privacy-preserving AI technology. One component is encrypted AI processing, designed to prevent providers from accessing users' prompts and responses in readable form. Another is cryptographic verification, which can provide evidence about the model, software, and computing environment used to process a request.

Illia compares the intended user experience to the security indicator in a web browser. People shouldn't need to understand the underlying cryptography to know whether an application provides verified privacy protections. Blockchain also provides a potential economic foundation for this system, allowing participants to hold tokens and access services rather than relying entirely on a single company.

Still, it’s concerning that more private AI could also make it harder to monitor harmful uses. Illia acknowledges safety as one of the strongest arguments against his approach, but believes privacy and security can coexist through better technical systems.

The Next Shift Could Be Bigger Than AI

Looking ahead, Illia is particularly excited about personalized medicine. He imagines a future where AI can analyze an individual's medical information and help develop treatments tailored to their specific needs, including therapies that might otherwise be commercially unattractive to large pharmaceutical companies.

He also expects AI to automate more activities where people primarily care about the outcome, while human experiences such as sports, music, and art retain their value because people care about the process itself.
Ultimately, Illia's believes that technology should expand what individuals can do without requiring them to surrender control over their lives.

As AI becomes more powerful and deeply integrated into everyday decisions, the bigger question won’t be how intelligent these systems can become, but who they ultimately serve.

👉If you enjoyed reading the summary, head over to When Shift Happens on YouTube or your favorite podcast platform to access the full convo.

quoted_text:
This week had more banging news items than Silicon Valley had tranched funding rounds.

The biggest news this week:

- Jensen Huang Investigation: What Happens Now
- Sequoia Leave London, Close Scout Program and End Evergreen Fund
- NASDAQ Loses $2.5TRN in 24 hours
- Anthropic targets $1.4TRN IPO valuation

My notes with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. What Is the Impact of Jensen Huang's Affair on China?

China is the big loser from the scandal. It will become harder to sell GPUs to China and to host them just across the border, and that route is likely to be shut down. The issue had already stalled in Congress.

2. Why the Anthropic IPO Will Trade Flat

Jason expects the Anthropic IPO to trade flat because the market is fatigued. Anthropic could not raise the full $100B directly in the IPO, and OpenAI was only able to raise $10B after tiring out its market. Retail demand is still hard to predict.

3. Why Are Anthropic in Such a Better Place Than OpenAI?

Anthropic will have its IPO done within a month, giving it the money and the float to leave private fundraising behind. Within six to nine months it could file a convertible and raise around $50B, with $200B on hand. OpenAI is still unprofitable, still private and still trying to raise $11B plus retail.

4. The Framework You Need to Adopt to Underwrite Zipline at $21BN

Zipline at $21B is unlikely to be justified on a revenue multiple. It has done three million US deliveries at probably $5 to $10 each, so it needs huge volume to work. The case rests on Zipline becoming the next infrastructure play, and at this price investors are leaning heavily on its Walmart contract.

5. The AI Trade Doesn't Crack on the Supply Side

The NASDAQ sell-off was largely reactive angst about data centers. Rory argues the AI trade holds through data center limits or NVIDIA ceding share to AMD as long as demand, evidenced in OpenAI and Anthropic ARR, is there. Hedge fund pods that lose their checkbook at a 5% drawdown and get fired at 7.5% were simply over their skis.

6. Why Did Sequoia End the Evergreen Fund?

The Evergreen fund rested on the sound idea that the real money is made after the IPO. But it launched in 2022 and 2023 as stocks fell, LPs have different liquidity needs, and partners who had already earned carry were forcing LPs to hold. Jason counters that holding generational assets like NVIDIA and Google for decades is the best idea in venture.

7. For Pre-AI Companies, It Really Is March or Die

Non-AI companies are still shipping at the same rate as in 2022 and 2023, and Jason has largely given up on them moving faster. He does not count Dialpad's $400M stock deal for Ada as an exit because there is no liquidity. AI-native companies will not buy these businesses either, since they are growing too fast to take on old contracts and their problems.

quoted_text:
I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used.

It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20.

These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs.

I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at https://t.co/YOtzND0Jqk.

There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.

text:
Today, Foreign Affairs publishes a long essay I wrote summarizing some of my work on the global fertility collapse:

https://t.co/pdQVTk8DnH

It was a fantastic experience (with great editorial support) because the essay pushed me beyond pure economics to discuss issues such as geopolitics and polarization. Unlike some commentators, I don’t think the first-round economic consequences of fertility decline matter most; the second-round political and social ones do.

Yes, social security systems worldwide are in danger, but reality will impose itself sooner or later. The same politicians who swear over their ancestors’ tombs that retirement benefits will remain untouched will cut them (even if they are French). It will not be pretty, and most likely the cuts will come only after a major crisis and after politicians have tried everything else and failed. 

Similarly, businesses will adapt to shrinking markets and valuations. Those who claim that capitalism somehow needs constantly expanding markets will be proven wrong. After all, this is the same misguided understanding of markets that has been proven wrong again and again since September 14, 1867, and that nobody really believes unless they have had the misfortune of earning a Ph.D. in a humanities department at an Ivy League school.

The real consequences will come when collapsing populations poison political systems. Look at the recent elections in eastern Germany. That is the future for all of us.

Also, the relative standing of great powers will shift drastically. Given current demographic trends, the U.S. will have a larger population than China by around 2100. The exact date depends on assumptions about net immigration into the U.S., but even with zero net immigration, the U.S. will overtake China by 2128. And Russia’s demographic future is only slightly more optimistic than China’s. 

Those who dismiss these changes forget how antiquity ended in Western Europe. The western part of the Roman Empire entered acute demographic decline around 200 CE. By 476 CE, the western empire no longer existed. Despite some revisionist views that have cast a more positive light on late antiquity (and rightly corrected what was sometimes an overly negative assessment of the period), the fact is that England or France in 600 CE had lost most of their classical heritage, and material life had lost at least an order of magnitude in sophistication. The eastern part of the empire, however, weathered its demographic collapse much better and lasted another millennium.

No, I don’t believe we will go extinct (the Amish and Haredi will be enough for the survival of humankind), but the world will be very different in 2200 regardless of how you feel about it. The rational is the real and the real is the rational.

text:
Be Jensen Huang:    

• Starts Nvidia in 1993. By 1996, the company is nearly bankrupt. He lays off half the staff and tells the team they are “30 days from going out of business.”

• In 1997, Nvidia wins a Sega contract, but Jensen realizes the chip won’t work. Sega invests $5M anyway, giving Nvidia six more months to survive and pivot.

• The pivot works. Nvidia goes public in 1999 and launches the GeForce 256, calling it the world’s first “GPU.” It goes on to dominate PC gaming.

• Jensen notices PhD students using Nvidia gaming cards for complex math. He realizes the GPU is much bigger than gaming and starts investing heavily in that future.

• Throughout the 2000s, Nvidia pours profits into developing CUDA, a software platform that makes GPUs programmable for AI, scientific computing, and many of the heaviest workloads that CPUs can’t handle. 

 • In 2016, Jensen hand-delivers Nvidia’s first AI supercomputer, the DGX-1, to Elon Musk for OpenAI to train a 'generative model'.

• In 2022, Nvidia stock crashes 66%. The PC market slows, Ethereum kills GPU mining, resale prices collapse, and revenue guidance falls. 

 • While the industry slows down, Jensen aggressively secures TSMC's limited CoWoS packaging capacity (the bottleneck for AI chips) betting the farm that the "big AI moment" is imminent.  

• In Nov 2022, OpenAI launched ChatGPT. Suddenly, every major tech company wants thousands of Nvidia H100s at $30K each.  

• From 2023 to 2025, big tech pours hundreds of billions into AI infrastructure. Nvidia becomes the choke point. CUDA keeps developers locked in.

• Nvidia becomes the most valuable company in the world, valued at $4.3 trillion, and Jensen owns approximately 3.5% worth $150+ billion.  

• Then everything starts to unravel. 

• On November 8, 2026, Nvidia’s board opens an investigation into Jensen’s relationship with a “Chinese spy” after he admits to an affair.

• On November 11, the NYT reports he also had an affair with Nvidia’s V.P of Healthcare, who reported directly to him.

• Today, Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately.

text:
On Sustaining a Protocol's Growth:

One thing most folks don't realise is how sustainability ultimately comes down to balancing both sides of the equation.

Most financial primitives rely on a two-sided market. The simplest example is an exchange, where every buyer needs a seller.

Finding PMF is one thing, but building a sustainable market that can scale requires structural demand from both sides.

@pendle_fi exemplifies this best through its novel primitives.

Yield Tokenisation (V2)

🔹Variable Yield Speculatoors (YT Buyers)  → Long on variable yields + upside from emerging yield narratives

🔹Fixed Yield Enjoyoors (PT buyers) → Lock in fixed yields at a discount, foregoing variable yield exposure

Two distinct participants with complementary objectives, creating a market where yield expectations can be continuously priced and traded.

This is what makes Pendle particularly interesting as a yield discovery platform, capturing new narratives as they emerge while reinforcing liquidity across both sides.

Boros @boros_fi

The same principle extends to funding rates, but with a different set of participants.

🔸Funding rate arbitrageurs → Seek to lock in attractive funding spreads, potentially across exchanges, while hedging their underlying perp exposure

🔸Rate speculators → Take the other side, positioning for changes in implied funding rates or the convergence of funding spreads

Arbitrageurs bring demand for hedging and locking in funding economics, while speculators provide the opposing exposure.

The parallel between V2 <> Boros is what stands out to me.

Pendle isn't simply creating new instruments to speculate on yield or funding rates, it's building markets where participants with fundamentally different objectives can transact with one another.

V2 transforms variable yield into a tradable market between fixed-yield seekers <> yield speculators.

Boros extends that framework to funding rates, connecting hedgers + arbitrageurs with traders expressing directional views on rates.

Different underlying markets, but same design philosophy of turning financial exposures into tradable primitives with natural demand on both sides that reinforces a dual-sided sustaining flywheel.

That's where the real scalability lies imo not just in capturing the next narrative, but in creating markets that remain useful beyond it.

The ticker is $PENDLE

7) cheap tokenization of huge speech corpora to train your own TTS or speech LM

8) game and XR characters that speak from the player's own device

9) offline assistive speech like voice banking and AAC devices, helped by a 4-bit decoder build that is 3.5× smaller

10) call-quality repair, where a small model predicts the tokens lost to dropped packets instead of playing silence.
