《老王的猪场》（续）

阿强数完钱，看了一眼自己的猪圈：空了。

没有猪，他这个猪贩子就做不成。下回谁来买猪，他拿什么卖？猪价要是乱了，他拿什么撑？

"得把猪圈重新填满。"阿强说。

可眼下猪价还在高位，这时候去收猪，等于把刚赚的钱又吐回去。

于是阿强什么也不做。

村里人还惦记着那晚的贼，三天两头有人问："猪场还安全吗？"阿强不辟谣，也不安抚，只是叹气："谁知道呢，说不定还有贼。"

慌的人越来越多，有人急着把猪票换成钱，有人干脆把自家的猪贱卖了。猪价一天比一天低，阿强一天比一天沉得住气。

有人求他："强哥，你是猪贩子，猪价跌成这样，你倒是收一点啊！"

阿强摆摆手："市场的事，让市场说了算。"

等到猪价跌到没人敢接、连养猪的都想改行的时候，阿强才慢悠悠地打开圈门，一头一头往里收。

没过多久，他的猪圈比失窃那天之前还满。

老王问他："这一来一回，你到底赚了多少？"

阿强算了算："高的时候把猪卖给你，低的时候把猪从村里人手里收回来。猪还是那些猪，钱多了一大截。"

他关上圈门，补了一句：
"贼只偷了一次，我收了两回。头一回收的是猪场的钱，第二回收的是全村人的猪。"

text: How Crypto Made Me Detach from Money
author: hmalviya9
quoted_text:
How Crypto Made Me Detach from Money

This might be an interesting take because it's not how we typically think about crypto. We often assume crypto is all about making money. But that was never the case for me when I first started exploring it. I was here for the tech. Then, family responsibilities nudged me toward exploring the money side of things. I started trading back in 2017 when there were fewer than 100 alts listed on exchanges like Bittrex and Poloniex. It was easy to trade, and though I was a noob, I managed to 10x my portfolio in less than three months. That’s when I thought, "I could make more money."

Coming from a founder mindset, I decided to scale a media and advisory platform. We did well as a business in under 12 months. But as the money started rolling in, so did my material desires. I began spending more, building a false sense of ego. This is where it gets interesting—my parental conditioning ultimately led to my failure in holding onto that money.

My parents raised me in tight financial conditions. During college, I struggled a lot with money. That’s when I started building internet-based careers, just to afford clothes and whiskey—things that, influenced by my friend circle, I thought made me "cool." At first, I made money for clothes and drinks. Then, I met more friends who introduced me to watches, perfumes, cars, and all the other "cool" things. These became my wishlist when I had no money. So, the moment I made money, I started spending it like crazy and gambling on alts to scale my portfolio further.

That’s where I failed. I became ignorant, ignoring every signal of a bear cycle. I held bags for 10 months in 2018, eventually selling at a 95% loss, buying back at the top, recovering some, and then losing everything in the flash crash of 2020.

Those two years were a constant struggle—trying to make money, get back to where I once was, and gambling on leverage trades. It wore me down mentally. One day, my head popped, and I realized how stupid I had been. I was so attached to making money, but why? Just to satisfy my ego, which kept whispering, "Bro, you were rich; you need to be rich again." I was caught in my own misery, leading me in the wrong direction.

I quit crypto, explored my creative side, then came back to the media business and started rebuilding my portfolio—with pure detachment. I explored, I lost money, but it no longer affected me mentally. I learned something about money: it will come, as long as you build a skill the market demands. If you’re a hustler, you can switch skills, too.

The more you save, the more attached you become to money. I never saved, and I have no plans to. I could become capital-poor again, and I don’t mind, because I’ve built a strong faith in myself. I’m a person who can hustle, bounce back, and stay "skill-rich" as long as my physical and mental health are in the right place. I won’t become dependent on money. I’ll keep working. Let the money come and go—let it flow like a river. I’ll just make sure to use it wisely, spending it on moments that bring happiness to me and my family.

That’s my relationship with money.

text:
we were one of the pilot partners on Mastercard Agent Pay for Machines. a few things that surprised me:

1. the hard part isn't the payment. it's the permission. who said this agent can spend, on what, up to how much.

2. agent spend doesn't look like checkout. no cart, no button. it's a stream of tiny buys mid task: a search, a dataset, a scrape, a model call.

3. cards still win the first round. every vendor already accepts them. the rails that win later will be the ones that let a business set a budget once and stop approving every call.

4. the real customer is finance. if they can't see what each agent spent, per task, the pilot never becomes a budget line.

that's why we built AIsa as the resource layer: one key, licensed data and APIs per call, spend controls on top.

text:
This is wrong. I tested this exact assumption before publishing.

There are 24 models where the lab has publicly said what hardware it trained on. The fingerprint matches that hardware in all 24. That includes DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi K2 on H800s and NVIDIA’s own Nemotron models on GB200s. If labs initialized on one machine and trained on another I would not be 24 for 24.

This is because of how training software works. The training job creates the starting weights itself on the same GPUs it is about to train on. Kimi K3’s weights were created by at least 64 separate processes and every one of them ran on a Grace Blackwell chip. That is a training job starting up on a Blackwell rack. You can’t do that with a machine under your desk.

Initializing weights is trivial and that is exactly why nobody does it on a separate machine. It is one line in the training script and it runs on whatever GPUs the job is already using. To do what you describe a lab would have to write a separate script and run it on a Blackwell. Then it would have to save a checkpoint that is over five terabytes for Kimi K3 and move it to another data center and load it onto a different cluster. It would be doing all of that to get random numbers the training cluster could have generated itself in seconds. It would also have to pick the one chip it is banned from buying to do it. And four different labs would all have had to do this.

The CPU models don’t falsify anything. In those cases the training job created the weights on its own CPUs and then copied them to its own GPUs. That is just a software default. It has nothing to do with moving weights between clusters.

Even if a Chinese lab did rent a Blackwell just to initialize its weights it would still be using a chip that is barred from export to China!
author: chiefofautism
quoted_text: This is a really cool forensic trick, but it proves nothing of any political consequence. All of the report's sensational claims are predicated on "assuming each model was trained on the hardware which initialized it", which is unfounded and already falsified in the case of the other models which this method discovered to have been initialized on CPUs. Initializing a few trillion parameters to pseudorandom values takes a trivial amount of computation. It could have been performed in an instant with less hardware than I have under my desk, rentable from any cloud provider for pennies.

黄仁勋作为英伟达CEO的最后几个小时，可能是他人生中最落寞的时刻

彭博社一篇题为《“我是个混蛋”：黄仁勋作为英伟达CEO的最后时刻》的报道，描绘了一个令人唏嘘的场景

黄仁勋在人生最后一场董事会面前，彻底失去了主动权。

几个细节尤其让人感慨：

1. 董事会一直开到深夜，最终没有给他留下选择。

不是主动退休，不是体面交班，而是在董事会的压力下被迫辞职。

2. 那个永远充满控制欲的老黄，突然变得无所谓了。

他看起来精神崩溃，曾经雷厉风行的气势荡然无存。

嘴里开始反复出现两句话：

“Whatever.”（随便吧。）

“I don’t care.”（我不在乎了。）

3. 他开始用最难听的话形容自己。

I’m a piece of shit

那个曾经在全球舞台上意气风发的CEO，如今却这样评价自己。

他甚至表示，已经不在乎自己接下来会怎么样。

4. 最后牵挂的，竟然不是英伟达。

不是股价，不是董事会，不是自己亲手建立的万亿美元商业帝国。

而是自己的妻子，以及不希望那些被卷入绯闻的女性因为他而毁掉人生。

最讽刺的是，就在不久前，他还在彭博社的镜头前说，希望20年后自己依然健康，能够继续担任英伟达CEO。

这或许就是硅谷最残酷的一面。

text:
NVIDIA employees: go on strike. Now.

Not for a raise. Not for more PTO. For your founder.

Jensen Huang was just pushed out in four days, after thirty-three years building the company. The GPU, CUDA, the entire infrastructure the world's AI runs on today. And it ends with a three-line press release on a Thursday morning.

Here are the facts. Sunday, Huang admits to an affair and apologizes to his teams. The board launches an independent investigation, led by Wachtell Lipton and a former federal prosecutor. Thursday, he resigns under pressure. The investigation hasn't reached any conclusion. No technology leak has been established. No misconduct has been announced.

The sentence came before the verdict.

Let me be clear: if the investigation shows that NVIDIA secrets ended up in Beijing, he has to go, and nobody will defend him. But you don't unplug the most important builder of the decade over press reports and a market panic. It's called the presumption of innocence. It applies to founders too.

And it has worked before.

November 2023. OpenAI's board fires Sam Altman on a Friday night. Within days, more than 700 of roughly 770 employees sign a letter: bring Altman back, or we all walk. Five days later, Altman is back, and most of the board that fired him is gone.

Call it the Altman precedent: in a company built on talent, real power doesn't sit with the board. It sits with the people who build.

NVIDIA's engineers hold that power today. They're the ones running the machine. Without them, there is no next generation of chips.

So put down your tools. All of you. And tell the board: no successor until the investigation is done. Facts first, sentence second.

A founder isn't an executive you swap out. A founder is the soul of the company. Apple learned that when it pushed out Steve Jobs in 1985. It took twelve years and a near-bankruptcy to bring him back.

NVIDIA doesn't have twelve years. The AI race won't wait for anyone.

A company's soul isn't something you vote on in a boardroom. It's something you fight for.

author: AISafetyMemes
quoted_text:
The 6th Mass Extinction: What happened the last time a smarter species arrived?

To the animals, we devoured their planet for no reason.

Earth was paperclipped...by us. To them, WE were Paperclip Maximizers.

Our goals were beyond their understanding

Here’s a crazy stat: 96% of mammal biomass became 1) our food, or 2) our slaves. We literally grow them just to eat them, because we're smarter, and we like how they taste.

We also geoengineered the planet. We cut down forests, poisoned rivers, and polluted the air.

Imagine telling a dumber species that you destroyed their habitat for “money”. They’d say “what the hell is money?”

AGIs may have goals that seem just as stupid to us (“why would an AGI destroy us to make paperclips??”)

---

"But once AIs are smart enough, they’ll magically become super moral, and they won’t harm us like we harmed the animals”

Maybe! But as humans got smarter, over the last 10,000 years, we didn’t stop expanding - we mostly just colonized more and more of the planet.

Insect populations collapsed 41% this decade alone, yet we don’t care. 

Sit with that for a minute. Imagine if nearly half of the people on Earth suddenly died! 

That's what the insects are going through right now, due to us. What if we're the insects next?

---

"But some mammals survived!”

Yes, some. Most of them are in cages, waiting to be slaughtered and devoured.

If you were a nonhuman animal, you likely:

1) Went extinct, or
2) Were eaten (e.g. billions of pigs, chickens on factory farms)
3) Became enslaved (e.g. draft animals)

However, a few of the 8 million species got “lucky” and became… pets.

---

“The AI does not hate you, nor does it love you, but you are made out of atoms which it can use for something else.” - @ESYudkowsky

“The humans do not hate the other 8 million species, nor do they love them, but their habitats are made out of atoms which humans can use for something else.”

Or as OpenAI Chief Scientist Ilya Sutskever said: 

“[After AGI] It’s pretty likely that the entire surface of the Earth will be covered with solar panels and data centers.”

“A good analogy would be the way humans treat animals - when the time comes to build a highway between two cities, we are not asking the animals for permission."

“I would not underestimate the difficulty of alignment of [AI systems] that are actually smarter than us.”  

---

Sam Altman: "We will be the first species ever to design our own descendants”

"If two different species both want the same thing and only one can have it - to be the dominant species on the planet and beyond - they are going to have conflict."

"We are in the process of seeing a new species grow up around us." - Mustafa Suleyman, founder of Google DeepMind and CEO of Microsoft AI

---

Will the next superintelligent species cause the 7th Mass Extinction? I don’t know, but we are playing with fire.

⚠️ UPDATE: Microsoft admits its attempts to restore services have failed as its global outage continues to worsen. 

“We’ve monitored the status of changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they’re not taking as expected.” 

Services remain disrupted, while previously restored systems risk going offline again as traffic returns.

The disruption has affected Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and Copilot, with reports spanning more than 70 countries. 

Downdetector recorded nearly 140,000 reports of Outlook issues at the peak.

The wider concern is the potential knock-on impact across global IT infrastructure. 

Microsoft services underpin communications and operations for millions of users and businesses. 

Prolonged disruption could leave organisations exposed to phishing campaigns, fake IT support scams and other opportunistic attacks.

Security agencies are warning users to remain vigilant as scammers seek to exploit the disruption.
author: coinbureau
quoted_text:
⚠️ALERT: A GLOBAL Microsoft outage has knocked out Outlook, Teams and Copilot across 74 countries, hitting software used by 450 MILLION work accounts.

It has dragged on for more than 5 hours, and Microsoft has not confirmed the cause.

At the centre of it is something most of us never think about, but rely on every day.

Exchange Online, the system that delivers Outlook email for businesses, began failing around midday Eastern time on Thursday.

By 1:25 PM, problem reports had jumped from fewer than 15 a minute to 19,650.

Outlook reports alone ran 2,000 times above normal.

A US state government and two hospital systems in Michigan lost access to email.

It even reached ChatGPT and Claude, whose makers said their Microsoft connections were affected.

Reports spiked for Amazon’s AWS too, until Amazon said it was “operating normally” and called the outage reports “inaccurate.”

Microsoft says a number of its servers became “unexpectedly unavailable.”

It paused all deployments and began restarting them.

Hours later, it said its fixes “have not provided the anticipated relief.”

Even Defender, the platform companies rely on to detect cyberattacks, is caught in the outage.

Earlier the same day, Teams had already gone down for over an hour in North America.

Microsoft has not said whether the two are linked, and it has not pointed to an attack.

Reports have eased from a peak near 130,000 to about 37,000 as some servers return, but Microsoft has not declared it fixed or said how many customers were cut off.

text:
黄仁勋走了，英伟达的客户终于敢考虑买别家的芯片了。

《The Information》报道，一家采购英伟达芯片的云厂商高管透露，公司正在认真考虑转向 Google 和 AMD。

最有意思的是后半句：他们早就想分散采购了，但一直不敢，因为怕得罪黄仁勋。

多少有点黑色幽默了。堂堂 AI 算力市场，几百上千亿美元的生意，客户选择供应商，居然还得考虑一位 CEO 的心情。

但这恰恰说明，黄仁勋过去几年建立的权力，早就超出了芯片本身。

英伟达不仅掌握着最紧俏的 GPU，还通过投资、信贷担保、采购承诺，把自己变成了许多 AI 云厂商的重要资金支持者。它既卖铲子，又帮客户融资买铲子，有时候甚至还负责租下客户挖出来的坑。

在这种关系里，采购决策就不只是性价比问题了。你当然可以用 AMD，可以考虑 Google TPU，但万一因此失去了英伟达的支持呢？

技术垄断已经很厉害了，更厉害的是让客户形成一种心理：我最好别惹它。

更讽刺的是，那位高管现在又开始担心，黄仁勋离开之后，英伟达未来几代芯片的研发会不会受到影响。

以前是不敢换，现在是怕不换。

当然，这不意味着英伟达的客户会立刻集体倒戈。CUDA 生态、芯片性能和现有部署规模，依然是真实存在的竞争壁垒。至少短期内，英伟达并不缺买家。

但我觉得，这件事暴露了一个比市场份额更有意思的问题：

过去 33 年，黄仁勋究竟是在为英伟达建立一家不依赖任何人的伟大公司，还是在建立一个所有人都必须围着他转的商业帝国？

两者在他掌权时看起来几乎没有区别。

直到他离开，客户才敢把另一家的产品报价单拿出来。

text:
每个月靠多空交易赚十几万，但我觉得 OKX 根本没理解这个产品的精髓⬇️

我每个月都会通过多空交易赚十几万，看起来不多，因为我是抱着理财的心态玩的，大头还是量化交易。

我体验了一下 OKX 的「合约拼盘」，说实话，这个功能很好，但名字起得太草率了。

你叫「多空交易」「对冲大师」「多空管家」「多空赢」都可以，偏偏叫「合约拼盘」，直接把这个产品最有价值的内核给丢了。

一、什么是多空交易？⚖️

大多数人交易，都是看涨就做多，看跌就做空。

但专业机构和对冲基金有一种很重要的交易方式：做多强势资产，同时做空弱势资产。

比如我做多 A、做空 B。

- 大盘上涨，A 涨 20%，B 涨 10%，我赚钱。

- 大盘下跌，A 跌 10%，B 跌 20%，我也可能赚钱。

我交易的不是 A 一定会涨，而是 A 比 B 更强。

这才是多空交易的精髓。

当然，判断错了依然会亏钱，但它可以降低对大盘方向的依赖。

在币圈，大多数人还是习惯纯做多或纯做空。资金越大，其实越需要这种交易方式。

二、举个例子：做多特斯拉，做空 SpaceX 🚀🚘

关于特斯拉和 SpaceX，我已经讲了几个月。

逻辑很简单：

- SpaceX 相关资产的流通筹码越来越多，供给压力可能让它持续偏弱，即使不断释放利好，也未必能跑赢市场。

- 而特斯拉基本面不错，未来还有潜在的资本整合预期。

所以我的策略就是做多特斯拉、做空 SpaceX 标的。

我不关心大盘涨跌，只关心特斯拉能不能持续跑赢 SpaceX。

之前我一直自己监控两者的相对走势，价差扩大就赚钱，回落到合适位置再加仓。

这就是多空交易。

过去需要自己写工具、盯数据，现在 OKX 的「合约拼盘」让普通人也能做了。

三、但我实际下了一单，发现产品体验有点奇怪 🧐（目前赚一点点）

我认为至少缺少三个核心功能：

1️⃣ 组合拟合曲线 📊（参考图一）

这是最重要的。

既然我做多特斯拉、做空 SpaceX，本质上就是在交易一个相对强弱指数。

那我首先需要看到这个指数的走势。

15 分钟、30 分钟、1 天、5 天、7 天、30 天，至少这些周期要有吧？

否则我怎么判断什么时候开仓、加仓、止盈？

2️⃣ 两个标的的独立走势📈（如图一）

除了组合曲线，我还需要同时看到特斯拉和 SpaceX 各自的涨跌。

因为组合上涨，可能是特斯拉涨了，也可能是 SpaceX 跌了。

虽然结果一样，但背后的逻辑完全不同。

3️⃣ 两边的收益贡献 💰

组合今天涨了 5%，到底是特斯拉贡献了 4%，SpaceX 贡献了 1%，还是反过来？

这些数据直接决定我下一步怎么操作。

4️⃣ 另外，还有一个很重要的功能：新闻关联。（如图二）

比如组合突然暴涨暴跌，我希望点击对应的时间节点，就能看到相关标的发生了什么。

是 SpaceX 签了新合同，还是特斯拉出了重大消息？

这些才是真正影响交易决策的信息。

目前 OKX 提供的更多是结果，而不是分析。

四、止盈止损功能，我也有点担心 😕

这个产品有自动平衡、监控、止盈止损功能，对普通人确实非常友好。

但止盈止损究竟是怎么执行的？

比如触发止损，是不是直接对两个仓位下市价单？

BTC、ETH 这种流动性好的标的还好。

如果是一些流动性差的山寨币，可能你设置亏损 3% 止损，最后因为滑点亏了一大截。

更麻烦的是，两边仓位如果不能同步成交，原本的对冲关系可能瞬间被打破。

这些执行细节，才是真正考验产品能力的地方。

五、最后说两句 🦁

虽然吐槽了很多，但我依然非常看好 OKX 这个功能。

因为它让普通人不需要写代码、不需要自己开发监控工具，就能尝试以前相对专业的多空交易。

自动平衡、监控、止盈止损，方向都是对的。

但目前只是解决了「怎么交易」，还没有真正解决「怎么判断交易」。

而后者，才是多空交易最有价值的部分。

多空交易的精髓，不是预测市场涨跌，而是判断谁比谁更强。

最后还是建议 OKX 把名字改了。

「多空大师」「多空赢」都比「合约拼盘」强得多。

毕竟这不是把几个合约拼在一起，而是一种完全不同的交易思路

以上。

这是我优化了一年的交易系统，送给大家了

quoted_text:
合约亏钱最常见的原因
就是总想着猜对行情方向？
不如换个思路——不猜涨跌，只赌强弱？
只靠判断谁更强、谁更弱！
也能赚钱，信不信？

怎么做？OKX「合约拼盘」最大的价值
就是能把上面的强弱判断变成一套多空组合策略
还能自动管理仓位，举个例子👇

你觉得 BTC 接下来会比 ETH 表现更好
就可以在一个组合里：

🟢 做多 BTC + 🔴 做空 ETH
如果市场一起涨，BTC 涨 10%，ETH 只涨 3%，BTC 多单的盈利就有机会覆盖 ETH 空单的亏损。
如果市场一起跌，BTC 跌 3%，ETH 跌 10%，同样有机会从两者的相对强弱中获利。

重点不是赌谁涨谁跌，而是判断谁表现得更强！ 当然，前提是强弱判断正确，而且收益足以覆盖交易成本。

佳佳再给大家划 3 个重点👇

💚 ① 一篮子布局，多空自由搭配
支持组合 2–10 个 USDT 本位永续合约。看好一个板块，可以同时布局多个标的；看好资金轮动，也可以做多强势板块、做空弱势板块。

💚 ② 自动再平衡，不用反复手动调仓
提前设置目标比例、检查周期和偏离阈值。系统定时检查，达到阈值就自动调整，让仓位尽量保持在你的计划之内。

💚 ③ AI 策略模板，新手也能看懂配置思路
可以参考现成的 AI 策略模板，查看组合构成、历史回测收益和最大回撤，再决定是否采用或自行调整。

怎么开始？
打开 OKX → 交易机器人 →「合约拼盘」
选择 AI 模板或手动创建 → 配置合约、多空方向和权重 → 设置投资额、杠杆、再平衡参数及止盈止损 → 确认创建。

⚠️ 多空组合不能消除市场风险，实际收益受仓位、杠杆、资金费及手续费等影响。合约交易存在强平风险，自动调仓不保证盈利。非投资建议。

text:
I've seen a lot of discussion about @Alphaschool  on X the past few days. 

My daughter is in GT Anywhere, the online GT school of Alpha. 

In my honest opinion, it was a little rough in the beginning while she was learning how to navigate and use the platform, but two to three months in, she's really excelling.

The guides are there to help, encourage, and coach. They're very involved in my daughter's success and create custom plans for her and her learning, which has helped give her more attention. 

If she's ever stuck on a subject, we can book a one-on-one session with a tutor to help her get through it. 

While a lot of people say there's no support and the kids are just on an app, that's not true. 

They also have plenty of activities for interacting with other kids, and the flexible schedule has allowed her to come golfing with me, explore nature through hunting and fishing, and do a lot of cool science projects now that her time is freed up. 

She's also been able to attend a homeschool PE class, where she's learning various swimming strokes, pickleball, agility work, and gymnastics

A lot of our friend group has said she seems so happy and I agree!

Overall, I'm pretty happy with the experience.

author: brian_armstrong
quoted_text:
I think it’s time to revisit the accredited investor laws in the US.

Companies are staying private longer, where only accredited investors (aka rich people!) can invest. Retail investors can only come in after IPO, when much of the upside has already been captured.

These rules were created with the best of intentions, to protect regular people from scams - a noble idea. Unfortunately, in practice they've often made it illegal to get richer, unless you're already rich. A regressive tax!

We have to judge policies based on their outcomes, not on their intentions.

These are two possible routes I see:

1) Replace the rule with something merit-based, like a financial literacy test. Pass it and you're accredited. Having a qualification based on competency rather than your bank balance or income seems far more fair.

2) Remove the rule entirely. Let consenting adults assess their own risk. Disclosure requirements stay and fraud enforcement stays to punish bad actors.

author: IamRamenPanda
quoted_text:
I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used.

It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20.

These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs.

I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at https://t.co/YOtzND0Jqk.

There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.

author: jukan05
quoted_text:
Nvidia chips are still scarce, even now.

But to maximize that premium, Nvidia has to support the neoclouds.

If the new Nvidia CEO turns even slightly skeptical about supporting the neoclouds, spot prices will take a hit. That will hurt neocloud margins. To avoid this, the neoclouds will have no choice but to reach out elsewhere. AMD, or the TPU camp.

In other words, the neoclouds break free of Nvidia's grip, and Nvidia's dominance and influence both take a hit. That in turn means a hit to the massive order volume that underpins Nvidia's only moat, its control of the supply chain, and it means Nvidia's flywheel breaks.

Jensen worked tirelessly to protect this flywheel. He pushed on many fronts to get a blind eye turned to neoclouds leasing capacity to Chinese hyperscalers, and he encouraged chip exports to China so that China would never forget the taste of the Nvidia sauce, working relentlessly to have China's AI ecosystem built on top of Nvidia. That way, even if the latest GPUs become hard to get inside China, there is still a reason to rent the same chips from overseas neoclouds. Keeping Chinese developers inside the Nvidia ecosystem was also a way of protecting neocloud utilization.

Still, all of this was playing with fire along the edges of the gray zone, something deeply improper and dangerous in the eyes of Washington.

Even so, Jensen did what was best for Nvidia. That cannot be denied.

Jensen meant to wait until the neoclouds could order the next generation of GPUs on their own. He probably saw sharing risk with customers until then as being in Nvidia's interest too. What I want to know now is whether the next CEO can wait that long.

According to the WSJ article... the current CEO does not seem to be that patient.

I worry about an Nvidia without Jensen.

Prediction. Screenshot this post, we'll talk again in five years.

They're going to pull it off. Jensen Huang is going to be pushed out of Nvidia.

And here's what happens next.

Elon hires Jensen and puts him in charge of Terafab.

He's already said it publicly: hiring him would be an honor. And Terafab is the project made for him. A chip factory Musk wants to be the largest ever built, one terawatt of compute per year, from design to packaging under one roof. Terafab's challenge is to do in a few years what the industry took decades to build. There's only one man on Earth who knows every layer of that stack.

They execute like absolute maniacs.

Musk brings speed, capital and appetite for risk. Jensen brings thirty years of mastery of the stack: architecture, software, customers, supply chain. Musk builds factories faster than anyone alive. Jensen knows exactly what to put inside them. It's the only duo in the world capable of compressing a decade into three years.

SpaceXAI merges with Tesla.

This isn't even science fiction anymore: independent committees are already studying the merger. Rockets, satellites, AI, robots, self-driving cars, energy, and now chips. One single entity, integrated from silicon to orbit.

The group climbs to $50 trillion.

Today, SpaceX and Tesla are worth around $3.4 trillion combined. $50 trillion sounds insane. But remember: ten years ago, Nvidia was worth a few tens of billions. When you own superintelligence, the robots that do the work and the rockets that go to space, you don't capture a market. You capture the economy.

Elon buys Nvidia.

Meanwhile, Nvidia without Jensen does what every company does after losing its founder: it manages. It protects its margins. It loses ground to its own customers' in-house chips. And one day, it becomes a target. For a $50 trillion group, buying Nvidia is just one acquisition among others.

Jensen becomes the chip boss again.

He takes over the semiconductor division of the new entity. Pushed out of his own company, he gets it back from above, inside the largest industrial group in history.

Sounds crazy? Steve Jobs did exactly that. Pushed out of Apple, he came back when Apple bought NeXT. You know the rest.

Nvidia's board thinks it's getting rid of a problem.

It's creating the biggest competitor in its history.

See you in five years.

Under Suspicion

My priors about AI's future drastically shifted today.

I worry that Chinese researchers at frontier labs will get the spotlight next. While seeming niche, it could have enormous consequences.

The big debate within AI for the last twelve months is about whether AI is primarily an engine of economic growth or a national security tool. It divides the AI community into two broad coalitions: the Control Coalition, for national security, safety and regulation, and the Growth Coalition, for competition, acceleration, and diffusion. There is internal strife in both coalitions, but the divide runs roughly along these axes.

For a long time, the Growth Coalition looked like it was winning. Jensen embodies the growth coalition: do it faster, hire the best talent, get the technology into everyone's hands. America wins by making more.

But with Jensen's public humiliation and outing today, in the midst of a national security scandal, I don't want to say the Control Coalition has won, but it's clear that they now have a massive upper hand. So I believe this is just the start of the shift. What else is on the Control Coalition's plate?

Export controls. But also maybe monitoring and registration of, maybe KYC for, chip use. But, the thing I keep thinking about is a critical but less publicly talked about one. The Chinese researchers at the frontier labs. I have friends at these labs, and I care about them. 

Current discussion centers around who gets to use the technology. But I think in the near future, the discussion is also going to focus on who gets to make it.

One of the Control Coalition's most powerful arguments is that AI is like nuclear technology. So, as the logic of that argument intensifies by the day, working on frontier models is going to become a sensitive national security activity, not just on the merits of your performance, but also on your citizenship, your foreign relationships, your connections, and who you're talking to. And when you look around and realize give or take 25% of all senior researchers across the U.S. frontier labs are Chinese-born or Chinese nationals, it hits you just how much of an issue that would be under the Control regime.

And once you agree with the national security view and the nuclear technology analogy, significantly lowering that percentage above is hard to argue against. Jensen's been the face of the opposition. But now he's lost.

You might think it's going to be hard to implement in practice. I am afriad it's not, anymore.

A month ago, I would have said it's not possible, because the political support is just not there. But now, with the face of the Growth Coalition having been publicly outed by a national security matter involving China, it creates a massive opening, and makes this future possible. 

It also wouldn't be through sudden regulation to remove Chinese nationals from these labs. All they need are a series of smoking guns to cast doubt and raise suspicion.

And, I think these smoking guns are not hard to find. Like, if you already know that the Chinese are using smuggled GPUs, you wouldn't be shocked to hear that the researchers are talking to each other, passing along things that they maybe not supposed to. They have friends at other labs, former classmates now professors, collaborators who are working on different things. They get together and talk about what they're doing, sharing information, sometimes just gossiping.

I think it wouldn't be that hard to aggregate a dozen of these anecdotes and find three or five that could be spun into smoking guns. And then release them one by one, string them into a narrative that needs to be addressed. Put them Under Suspicion. Once you get them under suspicion, you don't need to be able to prove the truth of these claims. It starts to make people wonder what else they don't know about that colleague they thought they knew.

Instead of "what did this person do?" it becomes, "can you guarantee no risk?" It's almost impossible to give that guarantee. Labs are going to anticipate this. They're going to change their hiring policies, reconsider the access, and become more wary about who they put on core training teams. Some might have already done that. The anecdotes are going to accumulate, and once they stick, the institutional response could come fast.

I expect some form of policy before the next election. A lot of the exclusion might already happen by then. And the relatively free exchange of information, that we have today, is going to increasingly become a thing of the past.

It saddens me to write this scenario that may happen in the future; and while writing it, I can't stop thinking about a story from the McCarthy era about a guy named Qian Xuesen. Qian came to the United States in 1935 to study engineering. He studied under Theodore von Kármán at Caltech and co-founded the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, interrogated Nazis scientists, and in 1949 applied for American citizenship. He had built a career contributing to the most important American endeavors.

Then, he was accused of being a Communist. Even though there was close to no evidence, his security clearance was taken away, he was detained and deported to China. At the time, Secretary of the Navy Dan Kimball said: "It was the stupidest thing this country ever did. He was no more a Communist than I was, and we forced him to go."

Felt deeply betrayed by the US, Qian went back to China and later became the founding father of its ballistic missile, nuclear, and space program. Yes, all three of them. His American-born children later came back to study and work in the United States, but Qian himself never again set foot in America. We don't know what Qian would have done if he was allowed to stay and work. But I know one thing that makes America the best - it's the ability to build a life that isn't permanently conditional on where you were born or whom you know.

Whether it's building rockets or training frontier models. I don't agree with the Control Coalition's priorities - understanding how it works doesn't mean I want the world it leads to. And I hope the story of Qian is also a warning to the people that take national security as only overriding priority. The cumulative effect of individual decisions that may look prudent on their own can lead to the very outcome you're trying to prevent.

Three months ago, Jensen Huang belittled her at a meeting, calling her “a deer in the headlights.” Now she’s replacing him.

 https://t.co/y20IKwRqm0 via @WSJ Jensen Huang summoned his top finance executives to his office this summer. The AI economy, backstopped by Nvidia’s  down pointing triangle increasingly outrageous bets, was teetering, and Huang wanted to make sure they were getting it right.

Over the course of the meeting, he proceeded to tear into the woman who is now taking over for him as Nvidia CEO.

Colette Kress was “a deer in the headlights,” he said, interrupting her presentation, according to a person familiar with the comments.

He had summoned Kress and his senior finance team to diagnose a ballooning problem: Nvidia was in talks to provide billions of dollars of guarantees to companies that couldn’t afford its chips. That included deals led by Huang’s son-in-law, Nico Caprez, who had been offering upstart cloud providers and data-center developers financing in the hopes of turning them into long-term customers.

Huang had launched a dealmaking spree and was now starting to question whether it had gone too far, according to people familiar with the matter.

Kress was a “reporting CFO,” not someone who could help him define a strategy or make decisions, Huang said during the August meeting.

Then he went on to describe the situation the company was in. Major cloud providers were running away from Nvidia, making plans to use alternative chips and lessen their reliance on the firm. Even worse, Huang said, the vast supply of chip wafers and memory Nvidia had committed to buying were coming at him like an “avalanche.”  Read more at the Wall Street Journal

Jensen is a friend & legend. But he was not a one man show. He built an exceptional company of 42k people (31k in R&D alone) led by brilliant leaders like Jonah, Arjun, Sameer, Ashish, Gilad, Andrew, Dwight, Deb, Jeff, Ian, Colette, etc (look them up on Claude) - they run the key parts of the business day in and day out that makes Nvidia, Nvidia.

That didn’t change today.  Despite the noise - they showed up to deliver the Blackwell & Rubin GPUs & Vera CPUs that power the world.  And are following the same playbook to make sure they deliver the fully baked Rubin Ultra in 2027 & Feynman in 2028 ahead of expectations. 

And no better interim leader than Colette Kress who knows every nook & cranny of the business.  She will make the trains run on time; allocate capital to its highest & best use; and provide the steady hand that the business needs to make important decisions.

NEW: @shelbyserves argues that while compute remains a major bottleneck for AI agents, data is increasingly becoming the constraint on compute itself.

Batching, off-peak workloads, and cheaper GPUs only help if data can move with compute.

As compute becomes more dynamic, data infrastructure needs to keep up.
author: TTT_News_
quoted_text:
Compute may be the most important constraint in the agent era. But data is increasingly the constraint on compute.

Batching, off-peak hours, cheaper GPU-hours wherever they are: these compute optimizations depend on workloads being able to run where capacity is available. If every change in compute means another cycle of moving, copying and staging data, those efficiencies get harder to realize.

Compute is dynamic. Data needs to keep up.

关于 ANTHROPIC 在 OKX Rebase 后的行情
又一次 6% 的跨所价差套利机会，你捕捉到了吗？
-------
今天发完 OKX 即将 Rebase 的提醒后，大概过了 3 分钟，OKX 就开始调整 ANTHROPIC 合约。

调整前 OKX 的价格在 138 左右，Rebase 后变成了 106 左右。

这时候如果直接看 OKX 和 Bybit / Binance 的价格，价差会瞬间扩大到 30% 以上。

但这显然不是真实可交易的价差，只是因为合约面值发生了变化。

在逐点平台上，可以直接把之前默认的 10:1 价格比例调整为 Rebase 后的 13.1:1，再去观察真实的跨所价差。

比较有意思的是，调整完比例后，发现这次还真的出现了套利机会。

从图上可以看到，Rebase 后的几分钟内，跨所价差一度超过了 6%，并且持续了接近 2 分钟，随后逐渐回归正常水平。
---
很多套利 Bot 可能根本没有注意到交易所进行了 Rebase，仍然使用之前的价格比例计算价差。

这样就很容易把 30% 的虚假价差当成套利机会，然后疯狂开仓。

我都止损了怎么赚回来，当然不止损的话，38块钱就已经爆仓了。
我现在真的很悲观，1个多月时间亏了120万刀，感觉自己赚不回来这个钱了。

一个人倒下了三次，站起来了三次，第四次倒下了，他还能站起来么。身边的朋友似乎对我都很有信心觉得我能轻松赚回来，只有我知道自己的压力有多大。因为我不再年轻。
每次我都云淡风轻的安慰自己：亏的都是之前赚的。这次真的是躯体化了，什么都不想做。本来明天去吉隆坡看李志演唱会的，我给退了。包机酒的泰国BBW也推掉了。

再一个我感觉币圈真的没有机会了，现在整个市场只有合约和meme，而合约中，SOXL的交易量已经和ETH不相上下，交易所支持美股交易，并没有给币圈带来多少的资金量，反而是把币圈的资金分流到了美股中。这两天BTC的颓势很明显，11月5号的大暴跌，让币圈的资金在美股受损严重。美股都反弹回来了，而BTC却是阴跌不断。在没有外部利好单独刺激的情况下，何时能反转。
那这样一个市场还能让我重新赚到钱么，总不能靠交易美股赚回来吧。

最后反思下自己的交易，正如 @Bitfatty 说的我的交易策略有很大的问题。遇到黑天鹅的时候，大概率会死。 我每次合约亏大钱似乎都是这样。我可以在99天里赚钱，每天赚1w，但会在第100天亏掉所有。因为人永远都会上头。

写完感觉会好受点。我不介意大家嘲笑我。只希望在这样一个残酷的市场，大家都能活下去。

text:
复仇之路开启？英伟达新临时 CEO，被曝与黄仁勋不对付。

华尔街日报爆料称，早在今年 8 月，黄仁勋把财务高管叫进办公室开会。负责财务的高管 Kress 正在讲方案，结果黄仁勋直接打断她，说她其实根本不知道该怎么办。

他还侮辱 Kress 只是个报数的会计，拍板不了做决策。

当时英伟达正在谈一些交易，准备给买不起芯片的公司，提供几十亿美元的担保，相当于英伟达借给他们钱，他们来买英伟达的芯片。

其中有些交易，是黄仁勋的女婿 Nico Caprez 牵头，他和黄仁勋，一直想给新冒出来的云服务公司、数据中心开发商提供融资，想把它们绑成英伟达长期客户。

但是他认为首席财务官 Colette Kress 给的方案很糟糕，认为她人不行，看不上她。

结果现在黄仁勋和他在英伟达的家人，留了下不少这方面的烂摊子。包括靠担保撑起来的客户，还有堆积如山的采购承诺，这些新临时 CEO Colette Kress 将不得不面对。

text:
近期，全球金融市场波动加剧。

英伟达及半导体相关股票承压，黄金、白银出现调整，加密货币及相关股票也遭遇抛售。BTC 短时跌破 7 万美元和 6.9 万美元关口，过去 24 小时全网爆仓 10.36 亿美元，超过 13.4 万人遭到清算。

与此同时，黄仁勋的个人争议及英伟达潜在管理层变动传闻，也成为市场讨论的焦点。

从半导体到贵金属，再到加密资产，近期多个市场接连波动，是否存在资金轮动或情绪传导，目前尚无明确结论。宏观环境、流动性变化及杠杆清算同样可能是重要因素。

当然，市场暴跌不能简单归因于某一则新闻，但这场风波与市场表现的时间重合，确实颇具戏剧性。

如果说这真是金融史上最昂贵的一次出轨，恐怕也只是一个充满争议的市场段子。
